text: Name an air vehicle that can fire S-8 80mm unguided rockets.
fact: The S-8 is a Soviet/Russian 80mm unguided rocket, usually fired from 20-round pods such as the B-8M1.
detail: Fixed-wing aircraft and helicopters. Any variant or export version counts; NATO and Russian names are accepted.

text: Name an aircraft that can fire 70mm (2.75 in) Hydra rockets or their predecessors.
fact: The Hydra 70 is an unguided 70mm (2.75 in) rocket, carried in 7- or 19-tube pods like the M260 and M261.
detail: Any 2.75 in / 70mm rocket pod, including older FFAR types. Fixed-wing and helicopters, any country.

text: Name an unmanned aircraft that can carry Hellfire missiles.
fact: The Predator was first test-fired with Hellfire missiles in early 2001, one of the first armed drones.
detail: Unmanned aircraft only. Any variant counts; manufacturer names and designations are accepted.

text: Name a fixed-wing aircraft that can carry the AGM-65 Maverick missile.
fact: The AGM-65 Maverick entered service in 1972 and comes in electro-optical, imaging-infrared and laser-guided versions.
detail: Fixed-wing aircraft only, any variant, any country. Helicopters don't count here.

text: Name a helicopter that can carry AGM-114 Hellfire missiles.
fact: Hellfire began as 'Heliborne, Laser, Fire-and-Forget', a missile built to kill tanks from helicopters.
detail: Helicopters only, including armed utility variants. Any model year counts.

text: Name an attack helicopter armed with a 30mm cannon.
fact: The Apache's M230 chain gun fires 30x113mm rounds and slews to wherever the gunner looks through a helmet sight.
detail: Attack helicopters with a built-in or chin/side-mounted 30mm cannon. Export versions count.

text: Name an aircraft that can drop the GBU-12 Paveway II laser-guided bomb.
fact: The GBU-12 is a 500 lb Mk 82 bomb with a laser-guidance kit, a mainstay of precision strikes since the Gulf War.
detail: Any aircraft that has dropped or been cleared to drop the 500 lb laser-guided bomb. Fixed-wing and drones; retired types count.

text: Name a fighter or attack aircraft that can carry the AIM-9 Sidewinder.
fact: The AIM-9 Sidewinder has served since the 1950s and is among the most-produced air-to-air missiles ever.
detail: Fighters and attack jets cleared for any AIM-9 variant, including older ones. Retired types count.

text: Name a tank with a 120mm smoothbore gun.
fact: The Rheinmetall 120mm smoothbore, and its licence-built M256 version, arms the M1A1 onward, the Leopard 2 and many others.
detail: Any tank fitted with a 120mm smoothbore gun, including licence-built and export versions.

text: Name an infantry fighting vehicle or armored vehicle armed with a 25mm cannon.
fact: The Bradley's M242 Bushmaster is a 25mm chain gun, also used on the LAV-25 and on ships.
detail: Tracked or wheeled vehicles with a 25mm autocannon. Variants and export versions count.

text: Name a tank or armored fighting vehicle with a 125mm main gun.
fact: Soviet 125mm smoothbore guns (the 2A46 family) arm the T-64, T-72, T-80 and T-90 lines, fed by autoloaders.
detail: Any tank or armored vehicle with a 125mm smoothbore gun. Soviet, Russian and licence-built versions count.

text: Name a tank or armored fighting vehicle armed with a 105mm rifled gun.
fact: The British L7 105mm rifled gun became a NATO Cold War standard, fitted to the Centurion, M60 and Leopard 1.
detail: Any 105mm rifled gun: main battle tanks, light tanks and wheeled gun vehicles.

text: Name a self-propelled (tracked or wheeled) howitzer armed with a 155mm gun.
fact: Barrel length in calibres matters: a 52-calibre gun like the PzH 2000 outranges a 39-calibre M109A6 Paladin.
detail: Tracked or wheeled self-propelled howitzers with a 155mm gun. Towed guns don't count.

text: Name an armored vehicle armed with a 30mm autocannon.
fact: A 30mm autocannon balances armour-piercing punch against light vehicles with ammunition weight and cost.
detail: Tracked or wheeled armored vehicles with a 30mm autocannon, from any country.

text: Name a disposable (single-use) shoulder-launched anti-tank weapon.
fact: Disposable launchers like the M72 LAW and AT4 are thrown away after one shot, trading reuse for low weight.
detail: Single-use launchers thrown away after firing. Reusable launchers like the Carl Gustaf don't count.

text: Name a main battle tank or tank-like fighting vehicle that uses an autoloader.
fact: Autoloaders let tanks run a three-man crew; many Soviet-pattern designs carousel the ammo under the turret ring.
detail: Vehicles whose main gun is loaded by machine rather than a human loader. Any country and era.

text: Name a tracked self-propelled air-defense system armed with surface-to-air missiles.
fact: Tracked air-defense carriers can keep pace with armoured columns, which truck-mounted systems often cannot.
detail: Self-propelled air-defense vehicles on tracked chassis that launch missiles. Wheeled systems don't count.

text: Name a weapon that the Su-30 can fire.
fact: The Su-30 has 12 weapon stations, and India's Su-30MKI has been modified to carry the BrahMos cruise missile.
detail: Missiles, bombs, rockets and guns the Su-30 family can carry. Name the weapon; designations and NATO names work.

text: Name a weapon that the F-16 can carry.
fact: The F-16's 20mm M61 Vulcan cannon sits in the left wing root, and it carries missiles on its wingtip rails.
detail: Munitions the F-16 can carry, across Block variants and operators. Pods and fuel tanks don't count.

text: Name a weapon that the A-10 Thunderbolt II can carry.
fact: The GAU-8 Avenger is a 30mm seven-barrel cannon; the A-10 was built around it.
detail: Munitions and guns the A-10 can carry. Pods and fuel tanks don't count.

text: Name a weapon that the AH-64 Apache can fire.
fact: The AH-64E can carry the JAGM, a Hellfire successor with a tri-mode seeker.
detail: Weapons the AH-64 Apache can fire, across A, D and E models.

text: Name an air-to-air missile with an active radar seeker.
fact: Active-radar missiles carry their own radar seeker for the final approach, so the launcher need not keep illuminating the target.
detail: Missiles with their own active radar seeker. Name the missile, not the aircraft that carries it.

text: Name an infrared-guided air-to-air missile.
fact: Infrared missiles home on heat, which is why flares are the classic countermeasure.
detail: Heat-seeking air-to-air missiles from any country, any generation.

text: Name an airborne early warning and control aircraft.
fact: AEW&C aircraft carry a large radar, often in a rotodome, to see low-flying aircraft beyond a ground radar's horizon.
detail: Airborne early warning and control aircraft, including helicopter and retired types.

text: Name an aerial refueling tanker aircraft.
fact: Tankers use a flying boom or a probe-and-drogue hose; the KC-46 can use both.
detail: Aircraft that can refuel others in flight, including buddy-refuelling and retired tankers.

text: Name an aircraft designed with low-observable (stealth) features.
fact: Stealth comes from shaping, radar-absorbent materials and internal weapons bays, not from any single trick.
detail: Manned and unmanned aircraft built around low-observable design, including prototypes and demonstrators.

text: Name an aircraft capable of vertical or short takeoff and landing (VTOL/STOVL), including tiltrotors and experimental types.
fact: The Harrier vectors its engine thrust through swiveling nozzles, while the F-35B pairs a lift fan with a swiveling exhaust.
detail: Anything that can take off or land vertically or in a very short distance, including tiltrotors and experimental airframes.

text: Name a military transport aircraft with a rear cargo ramp.
fact: A rear ramp lets these aircraft load vehicles on the ground and drop cargo or paratroopers in flight.
detail: Fixed-wing transports with a rear cargo ramp, any size or country, including retired types.

text: Name a helicopter with coaxial counter-rotating rotors.
fact: Coaxial counter-rotating rotors cancel each other's torque, so the helicopter needs no tail rotor.
detail: Helicopters with two rotors stacked on one mast turning in opposite directions, including demonstrators.

text: Name a ship-based anti-submarine warfare helicopter.
fact: Ship-based ASW helicopters drop sonobuoys and lightweight torpedoes such as the Mk 54.
detail: Helicopters flown from ships or used to hunt submarines, including older types.

text: Name a strategic bomber currently in service.
fact: The B-52 first flew in 1952 and is planned to keep flying into the 2050s.
detail: Long-range bombers currently in service with any air force.

text: Name an armed medium-altitude long-endurance (MALE) drone.
fact: MALE drones loiter for many hours at medium altitude, which makes persistent surveillance and strikes possible.
detail: Armed drones in the medium-altitude, long-endurance class, from any country.

text: Name a fighter or strike aircraft flown by the Indian Air Force.
fact: The Indian Air Force flies a mix of Russian, French and domestic designs.
detail: Fighters and strike aircraft the Indian Air Force has flown, current or retired.

text: Name a type of ammunition a main battle tank gun can fire.
fact: APFSDS 'darts' defeat armour with kinetic energy, while HEAT rounds use a shaped-charge jet.
detail: Name a type of round, not a specific model. Any era counts; Western and Soviet names both work.

text: Name a weapon mounted on the M1A2 Abrams.
fact: An Abrams carries a 120mm gun, a coaxial 7.62mm machine gun and typically a .50 cal on a commander's weapon station.
detail: Weapons mounted on the M1A2 Abrams, including remote weapon stations and grenade launchers.

text: Name an anti-tank guided missile.
fact: Javelin is a fire-and-forget missile with a top-attack mode; wire- and laser-guided designs need the operator to keep tracking.
detail: Guided anti-tank missiles of any generation and any country, launched from the ground or vehicles.

text: Name an 8x8 wheeled armored vehicle.
fact: 8x8 wheeled vehicles trade some off-road mobility for road speed and lower upkeep than tracked designs.
detail: Wheeled armored vehicles with eight driven wheels: APCs, IFVs and reconnaissance vehicles.

text: Name a man-portable air-defense system (MANPADS).
fact: MANPADS are shoulder-fired surface-to-air missiles; the Stinger and the Igla are among the best known.
detail: Shoulder-fired or crew-portable surface-to-air missiles from any country.

text: Name a self-propelled howitzer or gun that fires 152mm rounds.
fact: Russian 152mm artillery uses a different caliber from NATO's 155mm, so the ammunition isn't interchangeable.
detail: Self-propelled 152mm howitzers and guns, Soviet, Russian or other.

text: Name a multiple-launch rocket system (MLRS).
fact: Rocket launchers trade accuracy for volume: a BM-21 Grad fires 40 rockets in about 20 seconds.
detail: Rocket artillery launchers of any caliber or era, wheeled or tracked.

text: Name a main battle tank designed and built in Europe.
fact: European tank production is concentrated in a few families, and the Leopard 2 is the most widely exported.
detail: Tanks designed and built in Europe, including Cold War and retired types.

text: Name a tracked armored vehicle in service with the US Army.
fact: The AMPV is replacing the Vietnam-era M113 in US Army armored brigades.
detail: Tracked armored vehicles currently or recently in US Army service, including support vehicles.

text: Name a Soviet or Russian IFV or armored personnel carrier.
fact: The BMP-1, introduced in 1966, was the first mass-produced infantry fighting vehicle.
detail: Soviet and Russian IFVs, APCs and armored cars, tracked or wheeled.

text: Name a rifle chambered in 5.56x45mm NATO.
fact: 5.56x45mm NATO became NATO's standard rifle cartridge in 1980.
detail: Rifles chambered for 5.56x45mm NATO from any country. Carbine versions count as the same family.

text: Name a firearm chambered in .50 BMG (12.7x99mm NATO).
fact: The .50 BMG cartridge was designed around 1918 for the Browning M2 machine gun.
detail: Rifles and machine guns chambered in .50 BMG (12.7x99mm NATO).

text: Name a Chinese tracked armored vehicle.
fact: The ZTZ-96 and ZTZ-99 families form the backbone of China's modern tank force.
detail: Chinese tracked tanks, IFVs, APCs and self-propelled guns. Older types count.

text: Name an active protection system for armored vehicles.
fact: Hard-kill APS such as Trophy launch a countermeasure that destroys an incoming round before it hits.
detail: Hard-kill and soft-kill systems that protect armored vehicles from incoming missiles.

text: Name a Soviet or Russian jet fighter or interceptor.
detail: Any country-of-origin Soviet or Russian design: frontline fighters, interceptors and prototypes.
fact: The Flanker family (Su-27 and its descendants) was designed to match the F-15.

text: Name a fighter aircraft flown in World War II.
detail: Any nation, any variant. Prop fighters and early jets both count.
fact: The Spitfire's Merlin-powered design stayed in production for the whole war and beyond.

text: Name a jet fighter that flew in the Korean War (1950-53).
detail: Jets only, either side. Include Navy and Air Force types and Commonwealth aircraft.
fact: The F-86 Sabre and MiG-15 fought the first large-scale jet-versus-jet air battles over 'MiG Alley'.

text: Name a Cold War interceptor aircraft.
detail: Fighters built mainly to shoot down bombers: any nation, including retired types.
fact: The Mach 3 MiG-25 Foxbat was built to catch the XB-70 and shocked the West in 1976 when one was flown to Japan.

text: Name a fixed-wing aircraft that has operated from an aircraft carrier.
detail: Any navy, any era: fighters, strike aircraft, patrol, early warning and transports.
fact: Catapult launches and arrested landings put enormous stress on carrier aircraft, so they are built with heavy landing gear and strengthened airframes.

text: Name an electronic warfare or SEAD (suppression of enemy air defenses) aircraft.
detail: Dedicated jammers, 'Wild Weasel' radar hunters and aircraft modified to carry anti-radiation missiles.
fact: The Wild Weasel mission began in Vietnam, when F-100F and F-105F crews hunted SA-2 radars on purpose to draw them off other strikers.

text: Name an anti-radiation missile (ARM) that homes on enemy radar emissions.
detail: Air-launched missiles of any country and era designed to hunt radar emitters.
fact: An anti-radiation missile rides the enemy radar's own signal down to its source, which is why operators sometimes shut radars off instead of risk them.

text: Name an air-launched cruise missile.
detail: Standoff missiles launched from aircraft that fly to the target on a guided, low flight path. Both nuclear and conventional types count.
fact: Cruise missiles fly like small jets, so unlike ballistic missiles they can follow the terrain at low altitude.

text: Name a precision-guided air-dropped bomb or guidance kit.
detail: Laser-, GPS- or TV-guided bombs and glide kits from any country, including historical types.
fact: The JDAM isn't a new bomb at all: it's a GPS tail kit that turns an ordinary Mk 82, 83 or 84 into a guided weapon.

text: Name an unguided (gravity) bomb or cluster bomb.
detail: Bombs of any country and era without a guidance kit, including cluster and runway-attack munitions.
fact: The Mk 80 series (Mk 81, 82, 83, 84) is the backbone of Western bomb stocks, and the bombs that guidance kits like JDAM turn into smart weapons.

text: Name a medium or heavy military transport helicopter.
detail: Helicopters built to carry troops or cargo, including heavy-lift and retired types.
fact: The Mi-26 Halo is the heaviest production helicopter ever built, able to lift around 20 tonnes.

text: Name a manned reconnaissance or surveillance aircraft.
detail: Spy planes and signals-intelligence aircraft, including types adapted from fighters and airliners.
fact: The SR-71 Blackbird flew faster than Mach 3, and outran missiles by simply flying away from them.

text: Name a maritime patrol or anti-submarine fixed-wing aircraft.
detail: Long-range sea patrol aircraft, including flying boats and retired types.
fact: The P-8 Poseidon is a militarized Boeing 737, replacing the turboprop P-3 Orion.

text: Name a fixed-wing gunship.
detail: Side-firing cargo aircraft converted into gunships, from Vietnam-era types to modern versions.
fact: A gunship circles its target in a pylon turn, so its side-firing guns keep hitting the same spot.

text: Name a dedicated ground-attack or close air support aircraft.
detail: Aircraft designed or primarily used to attack targets on the ground, of any country and era.
fact: The A-10 and Su-25 were both designed to survive heavy ground fire, with titanium armour around the cockpit.

text: Name a jet trainer aircraft.
detail: Advanced trainers and lead-in fighter trainers, including light-attack derivatives.
fact: The BAE Hawk has trained pilots since 1976 and also flies as the Red Arrows' display aircraft.

text: Name an attack helicopter (any country).
detail: Purpose-built or armed attack helicopters of any country, including retired and prototype types.
fact: The AH-1 Cobra, introduced in 1967, was the first dedicated attack helicopter.

text: Name a military aircraft designed or built in China.
detail: Fixed-wing aircraft and helicopters designed or built in China, including licence-built, retired and export types.
fact: The J-20 is the first operational fifth-generation fighter fielded outside the United States.

text: Name a jet fighter or fighter-bomber designed in Europe.
detail: Jet-age fighters and strike fighters from any European country, including retired types.
fact: Europe's Eurofighter, Rafale and Gripen are all canard-delta designs, built around very different national requirements.

text: Name a weapon that the AH-1Z Viper can fire.
detail: Missiles, rockets and guns cleared for the AH-1Z, including those on its wingtip rails.
fact: The AH-1Z's wingtip stations carry AIM-9 Sidewinders, giving a helicopter a real air-to-air option.

text: Name a weapon that the Eurofighter Typhoon can carry.
detail: Missiles, bombs and guns cleared for the Typhoon with any user air force.
fact: Typhoon carries Meteor and AMRAAM missiles on semi-recessed fuselage stations to reduce drag.

text: Name a weapon that the Rafale can carry.
detail: Air-to-air, air-to-ground, anti-ship and nuclear weapons cleared for the Rafale.
fact: The Rafale was designed to carry up to 9.5 tonnes of external stores on 14 hardpoints.

text: Name a weapon that the F-35 can carry.
detail: Weapons integrated or cleared for the F-35 in any version, internal bays or external stations.
fact: The F-35's GAU-22/A is a four-barrel 25mm cannon, internal on the A model and carried in a pod on the B and C.

text: Name a heavy or strategic bomber from any era.
detail: Large long-range bombers from World War II to today, including types that never entered service.
fact: The B-52 and the Tu-95 Bear are both 1950s designs that remain in front-line use.

text: Name a variable-sweep ('swing-wing') aircraft.
detail: Aircraft whose wings sweep back for speed and forward for slow flight: fighters, bombers and experimentals.
fact: The wings of an F-14 Tomcat sweep automatically from 20 to 68 degrees as speed changes.

text: Name a fighter or bomber with canard foreplanes.
detail: Aircraft with small wings ahead of the main wing, in any era, including those with canards as a control surface.
fact: Canards put a small lifting surface ahead of the wings, trading some stability for agility.

text: Name a delta-wing military aircraft.
detail: Triangular-wing aircraft, including fighters, interceptors and bombers, with or without canards.
fact: The delta wing's long root chord is strong and stiff, which suits high-speed interceptors like the Mirage III and F-106.

text: Name an aircraft-mounted gun or autocannon.
detail: Cannons and machine guns used on fixed-wing aircraft or helicopters, in any era.
fact: The M61 Vulcan, a six-barrel 20mm rotary cannon, has been the standard US fighter gun since the late 1950s.

text: Name a tank used in World War II.
detail: Any nation's tanks, light, medium and heavy, including prototypes that saw combat trials.
fact: The T-34 combined sloped armour, a powerful gun and wide tracks, and shaped tank design for the rest of the war.

text: Name a World War II tank destroyer or assault gun.
detail: Turretless or casemate fighting vehicles built to kill tanks or support infantry, from any nation.
fact: The StuG III was built as an infantry-support gun but ended up destroying more tanks than any other German armored vehicle.

text: Name a United States tank, light or main battle.
detail: Any US-designed tank from World War II to today, including prototypes that entered service.
fact: The M60 Patton served from 1960 into the 1990s and was the US Army's main battle tank until the M1 Abrams replaced it.

text: Name a Soviet or Russian tank.
detail: Light, medium, heavy and main battle tanks from the interwar years to today.
fact: More T-54/55 tanks were built than any tank in history, with around 100,000 produced.

text: Name a military sniper rifle.
detail: Bolt-action and semi-automatic sniper rifles in military service, in any era and any caliber.
fact: The Dragunov SVD (1963) was designed as a squad-level designated marksman rifle rather than a bolt-action sniper rifle.

text: Name a machine gun used by a military.
detail: General-purpose, light, medium and heavy machine guns from any era and country.
fact: The German MG 42 fired around 1,200 rounds a minute, and its design is still used in the modern MG3.

text: Name a military service pistol.
detail: Standard-issue handguns of any army or navy, past or present.
fact: The M1911 served as the US military sidearm for more than 70 years.

text: Name a submachine gun.
detail: Pistol-caliber automatic weapons of any country and era, including those from the World Wars.
fact: The Thompson submachine gun's 'Tommy gun' nickname came from its inventor's own name.

text: Name a 7.62x51mm NATO battle rifle or designated marksman rifle.
detail: Full-power rifles chambered in 7.62x51mm NATO, from the Cold War to today.
fact: The FN FAL was adopted by more than 90 countries and was nicknamed 'the right arm of the Free World'.

text: Name an AK-pattern rifle or Kalashnikov derivative.
detail: Rifles built on the Kalashnikov action, from the original AK-47 to modern Russian and foreign derivatives.
fact: The AK-47 is the most produced firearm in history; estimates run to 100 million rifles.

text: Name a grenade launcher (underbarrel, handheld or automatic).
detail: 40mm and other grenade launchers of any country, including crew-served automatic types.
fact: The M79 'Thumper' fired a 40x46mm grenade; the later M203 let infantry carry the launcher under a rifle.

text: Name a mortar system or mortar carrier.
detail: Infantry, towed and vehicle-mounted mortars of any caliber, including historical siege mortars.
fact: Mortars lob shells at steep angles, so they can hit targets hidden behind hills or buildings.

text: Name an anti-aircraft gun or self-propelled anti-aircraft gun (SPAAG).
detail: Towed and self-propelled gun-based air defense of any caliber and era, including land-based C-RAM systems.
fact: The ZSU-23-4 Shilka's radar-guided quad 23mm cannons made it deadly to low-flying aircraft.

text: Name an armored reconnaissance vehicle.
detail: Wheeled and tracked scout vehicles and armored cars of any country and era.
fact: The Scorpion/Scimitar family of light tracked vehicles was built to be quiet and fast on the battlefield.

text: Name a light tank.
detail: Light tanks and air-portable gun vehicles of any country and era.
fact: Light tanks trade armour for speed and weight: the M551 Sheridan could even be parachuted.

text: Name an armored engineering, bridge-laying or recovery vehicle.
detail: Combat engineer vehicles, bridgelayers, mine-clearers and armored recovery vehicles of any country.
fact: Armored bridgelayers can span a ditch up to around 20 metres wide in just a few minutes.

answers.name: Challenger ARRV
aliases: Challenger Armoured Repair and Recovery Vehicle

text: Name a towed howitzer or field gun.
detail: Towed field artillery of any caliber, from the World Wars to today.
fact: The M777 lightweight howitzer uses titanium to cut weight to about 4.2 tonnes, so helicopters can lift it.

text: Name an anti-tank gun (towed).
detail: Towed anti-tank guns of any caliber and era, including World War II types.
fact: The German 8.8 cm Pak 43 could knock out any Allied tank of its day from over a kilometre away.

text: Name a surface-to-air missile system (any range).
detail: Ground-based air-defense missile systems of any country, from short-range to long-range, including retired ones.
fact: The S-75 Dvina shot down the U-2 flown by Gary Powers in 1960.

text: Name a tactical or short-range ballistic missile or rocket.
detail: Land-based short-range ballistic missiles and large artillery rockets of any country and era.
fact: The V-2, first used in combat in 1944, was the world's first long-range ballistic missile.

text: Name a Western infantry fighting vehicle.
detail: IFVs designed in NATO or allied countries, tracked or wheeled, current or retired.
fact: The Bradley was designed to carry an infantry squad and fight alongside tanks, with a 25mm cannon and TOW missiles.

text: Name an MRAP or mine-resistant armored vehicle.
detail: Mine-Resistant Ambush-Protected vehicles and similar V-hull protected vehicles from any country.
fact: MRAP vehicles use a V-shaped hull to deflect the blast of roadside bombs away from the crew.

text: Name a tracked armored personnel carrier.
detail: Fully tracked APCs of any country and era (not wheeled, not IFVs).
fact: The M113 was introduced in 1960 and has been built in more than 80,000 units.

text: Name an amphibious military vehicle.
detail: Land vehicles able to swim: APCs, IFVs, light tanks and cargo carriers, from World War II to today.
fact: The DUKW, introduced in 1942, was an amphibious truck that carried supplies from ships to shore.

text: Name a round fired by the Abrams' 120mm M256 gun.
detail: Ammunition types the 120mm smoothbore of the M1A1/M1A2 can fire, including training rounds.
fact: The M829 family of depleted-uranium-core sabot rounds is the Abrams' main anti-tank ammunition.

text: Name a weapon fitted to the M2/M3 Bradley or its variants.
detail: Guns and missiles on Bradley IFVs, CFVs and air-defense variants such as the M6 Linebacker.
fact: The Bradley's TOW launcher lets a vehicle that carries infantry also knock out tanks from over 3 km.

text: Name a weapon fitted to the T-90 tank.
detail: Armament on the T-90, T-90A, T-90S and T-90M, including the main gun, missiles and secondary weapons.
fact: The T-90's 125mm gun can fire a 9M119 laser-guided missile through its barrel.

text: Name a reusable shoulder-fired rocket or recoilless launcher.
detail: Reloadable anti-armor and anti-bunker launchers of any country and era (not disposable, not guided missiles).
fact: The RPG-7, designed in 1958, remains one of the most widely used anti-tank weapons in the world.

text: Name a military camouflage pattern.
detail: Named patterns used by armed forces, from digital and woodland designs to historical field patterns.
fact: Digital camouflage such as MARPAT and CADPAT breaks up an outline with small square pixels rather than blotches.

text: Name a military helmet.
detail: Helmets from any army, from the First World War to today.
fact: The German Stahlhelm, introduced in 1916, defined the look of the steel helmet and was copied or adapted worldwide.

answers.name: PASGT
aliases: Personnel Armor System for Ground Troops

text: Name a light tactical or utility vehicle used by militaries.
detail: Jeeps, light trucks and armored utility vehicles of any country, from World War II to today.
fact: The Willys Jeep gave its name to a whole class of vehicle: some 640,000 were built in World War II.
